newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines' Ramos defends privatisation deals.
newsitem.headline: Philippines' Ramos defends privatisation deals.

text.p: The Philippines has one of the most liberal privatisation programmes in the Asia-Pacific and foreign investors who complain about it may not have done their homework, President Fidel Ramos said on Thursday.
"It is one of the most liberal systems existing in the Asia-Pacific today," Ramos told a lunch meeting with reporters.
Several high-profile privatisations have become bogged down in legal or procedural wranglings, including the sale of the historic Manila Hotel where the lunch meeting was held.
The government-owned hotel, headquarters of World War Two U.S. General Douglas MacArthur, was supposed to have been sold to Malaysian firm Renong Bhd at an auction last year.

But one of the losing bidders, a Manila newspaper publisher, challenged the result through the Philippine Supreme Court, arguing that the hotel was a national monument and should have been sold only to Filipinos.
Ramos himself intervened last month in a dispute over the privatisation of the Subic Bay container terminal north of Manila, ordering a review of all the bids.
Foreign businessmen and diplomats have been vocal in their complaints, arguing that delays and uncertainties discourage the overseas investment that Ramos is eager to attract.
Foreign investors should ensure they understand Philippine procedures and that sometimes these projects were subject to review either by the government or through the courts, Ramos said.

"I'm sure our foreign friends will not begrudge us that final step that must be taken under our system of laws. Some of them may not have that final step under their laws but we do have it here," he said.
"It is probably the lack of the completion of the due process or the due diligence aspect of that process that created these problems," he said.
Ramos said the Philippines provided varied ways for foreign firms to invest here in privatisations or development projects.
These include build-operate-transfer projects, long lease arrangements and joint ventures.
The power sector demonstrated the success of these policies, said Ramos, who took office in 1992 amid a power crisis involving blackouts for up to 10 hours daily.
The government now had more power project proposals from the private sector than it needed and had to be careful it did get an over-supply, he said.
